decathlon-wizard.title: From abandoned forms to self-published trips
decathlon-wizard.subtitle: Decathlon Travel · Partner SaaS
decathlon-wizard.heroTitle: From abandoned forms to self-published trips
decathlon-wizard.heroSubtitle: Redesigning the trip creation experience for travel experience providers — from discovery to delivery — to make publishing a trip on Decathlon Travel faster, simpler, and scalable.

ataGlance.intro: Decathlon Travel is a marketplace for sports trips — climbing, skiing, surf camps, guided hikes. Partner is the B2B SaaS used by travel experience providers to manage and publish their trips on the platform.
ataGlance.myRole: As Product Designer, I led the research structure, workshops, and design direction. Discovery, testing, and key decisions were co-constructed with a PM.
ataGlance.timeline: 3–4 months · Startup mindset — ship fast, iterate
ataGlance.team: Reduced team · 3 devs (2 back-end, 1 front-end) · Running in parallel with a UI compliance overhaul and UX quick wins on the existing Partner interface

genesis.title: The genesis
genesis.body: The company wasn’t converting enough — trips weren’t selling at the expected rate. Leadership decided to shift focus toward the B2B side of the product, with the goal of growing the number of trips available on the platform. My research findings from the search bar project were one of the inputs for that shift: interviews and analytics showed that users weren’t finding what they wanted because there simply weren’t enough trips listed. When the focus moved to the Partner tool, I dug deeper into how trips were being added to the platform and raised it in the product team’s weekly meeting. Once the team aligned, it was added to the next quarter’s roadmap — and I began discovery and user research in parallel with the already-agreed UX work.

genesis.title: The real problem
genesis.body: Partners were struggling to publish trips. Surveys and interviews with internal teams and travel experience providers revealed a consistent picture: no guidance, no sense of progress, no way to save and return. 78.6% spent 40+ min on a single trip — many gave up entirely.

genesis.title: The scope
genesis.body: An end-to-end redesign of the trip creation experience — from discovery and research through to design, testing, and delivery. The goal was to make publishing a trip significantly easier for travel experience providers. Running in parallel with a UI compliance overhaul on the existing Partner interface.

genesis.title: The outcome
genesis.body: A guided wizard that allowed 78% of partners to publish their trips entirely without assistance — contributing to a +283% increase in trips on the platform over the 10 months following deployment.

kpis.description: Trips published over the 10-month period following deployment
Saved per week per advisor (internal survey)

timeline.title: Prior focus
timeline.body: My main focus was B2C — conversion optimisation and features such as user account, insurance, and sports level indicators. Research conducted during the search bar redesign surfaced a supply gap: users weren’t finding enough trips. I presented these findings to leadership, which contributed to a broader strategic shift toward the B2B side of the product.

timeline.title: Audit & quick wins
timeline.body: I onboarded onto the Partner tool through assigned UX work — a UI compliance overhaul and prioritised screen fixes. In parallel, I began informal discovery: a product audit and internal team interviews to build a baseline understanding of the partner experience.

timeline.title: Discovery & research
timeline.body: I led the formal user research phase — partner interviews, internal team interviews, and a survey (n=14). This uncovered the core pain points: no guidance, no sense of progress, no save state, and an overwhelming number of fields with no clear sense of priority.

timeline.title: Design & delivery
timeline.body: Working alongside the PM and dev team, I drove workshops, design exploration, trade-offs, prototyping, and iterative delivery. Key decisions included the mandatory/optional field split, the logical flow, the guidance system, and the pricing approach.

timeline.title: Deployment
timeline.body: The redesigned experience shipped. 78% of partners became fully self-sufficient. Over the following 10 months, trips published on the platform increased by +283%.

discovery.problemStatement: The company had shifted to a B2B focus, and the priority was clear: how can we make adding a trip to the platform faster and less painful for travel experience providers? Adding a trip was a well-known, long-standing pain point — time-consuming, frequently abandoned, and a direct blocker to growing supply on the platform.
discovery.context: The Partner tool had been built with little to no UX oversight. Features had been added incrementally without a structured design process, which explained much of what we found.
discovery.methods: Internal team interviews · Partner interviews · Partner survey (n=14) · Benchmarking exercise (n=4) · Product audit

stats.label: Of partners spent 40+ min creating a single trip
Identified "Programme" as the most time-consuming section

discovery.advisorCallout: Every new partner onboarding included a 30-minute session with a travel advisor — covering the entire tool, not just trip creation. When partners got stuck, they called for help. Advisors would sometimes fill in the form themselves, and prices were occasionally entered manually after partners sent them a spreadsheet. A significant portion of advisor time was spent compensating for what the tool should have handled.

insights.title: Flawed first-time user experience
insights.body: The onboarding session covered the entire tool — orders, trips, finances, settings — leaving little time to properly walk through trip creation. Partners were largely left to figure it out on their own.

insights.title: Cognitive overload
insights.body: An overwhelming number of fields with no way to distinguish mandatory from optional, no save state, and no sense of progress. Abandonment was common.

insights.title: Compensating behaviours
insights.body: Travel advisors were filling in forms on behalf of partners, entering prices manually from spreadsheets, and spending hours per week on tasks the tool should have handled independently.

designDelivery.fromResearchToDirection: The research findings pointed clearly toward the core issues: no guidance, no sense of progress, and an overwhelming number of fields with no clear priority. Two directions were considered: enhancing the existing interface, or a step-by-step wizard. Given the volume of mandatory information, the length of the task, and the varying levels of technical confidence among partners, the wizard addressed all outstanding problems simultaneously. It was unanimously agreed upon in the weekly product meeting.
designDelivery.mandatoryWorkshop: Before any design work began, I led a cross-functional workshop to establish what information was truly necessary. In the room: the CTO, two developers, the PM, the content manager, a travel advisor, and an account manager. Using card sorting, we went through every field and defined what was mandatory from a technical standpoint, useful for end users, and what could be made optional or removed. The output was a consolidated field list — ensuring partners only faced what was truly necessary.

decisions.title: Logical flow
decisions.body: Steps were ordered around how partners naturally think about their trips: experience details first, then the programme, then logistics. Not around how the database was structured.

decisions.title: Guidance system
decisions.body: Save state, progress bar, placeholder text, character counts, and contextual help throughout. Confirmed technical feasibility with the dev team before committing to the direction.

decisions.title: Live preview
decisions.body: As partners filled in information, they could see how their trip would appear on the marketplace. An immediate feedback loop that gave partners a reason to care about content quality.

decisions.title: The hard call — Pricing
decisions.body: Two trip types, prices varying by season, group size, and age, with nested add-ons. The solution was a dynamic grid: partners would first answer questions to define their pricing parameters, which would generate a tailored grid for them to fill in. Early dev conversations meant constraints were surfaced before they could block the solution.

designDelivery.userTesting: Two rounds — one internal session and one with two partners, conducted by the PM using my test plan. Testing focused on validating that the wizard felt intuitive, reduced cognitive load, and gave partners a clear sense of progress.
designDelivery.workingWithDevs: Developers were brought in early and kept in the loop throughout — not just at handoff. The PM and I co-wrote Jira tickets using a template I had built with the dev team. Wireframes and prototypes were linked directly in the tickets.

impact.opening: Shipping the redesigned experience had a measurable effect on both sides of the platform — for the partners using it, and for the internal teams supporting them.
impact.closingQuote: The +283% increase in trips published over the 10 months following deployment reflected a platform that was finally easier to contribute to. But the number I’m most proud of is the 78%. Partners — many non-tech-savvy, many running solo businesses — could publish their experience on a marketplace entirely on their own. That’s what a well-designed product should do.
impact.whatIDoDifferently: The pricing section deserved a dedicated sprint rather than being absorbed into the overhaul. Starting the Partner immersion before the search project concluded would also have accelerated the discovery phase significantly.

decathlon-wizard.myRole: Product Designer in a duo with a PM, alongside backend dev, frontend dev and CTO. End-to-end scope — from discovery to delivery.
decathlon-wizard.context: Decathlon Travel is a marketplace for sports trips. Experience providers use a B2B SaaS called Partner to manage bookings, payments, and list their trips on the marketplace.
decathlon-wizard.problem: 78.6% of partners spent more than 40 minutes creating a trip. The form was a single overwhelming page with no progress indicator, no guidance, and everything appearing mandatory.
decathlon-wizard.solution: A step-by-step wizard replacing the monolithic form, with mandatory/optional split, logical flow, save state, progress bar, and live preview.

stellaris-ftue.title: Talent First
stellaris-ftue.subtitle: Global B2B SaaS · Data UX
stellaris-ftue.context:
This project focused on an enterprise market research platform with a large and mature feature set.

The product originally existed as a desktop application and was difficult to learn and use. Most users relied on training and internal experts, as very little of the system was intuitive.

The business goal was to make this powerful product accessible, scalable, and suitable for SaaS, without losing its core functionality.
stellaris-ftue.myRole:
Senior Product Designer responsible for process modeling, workflow design, interaction principles, and cross-role system behavior.

Led the UX transformation of a complex enterprise product, moving it from legacy workflows to a scalable SaaS foundation.
stellaris-ftue.problem:
As the product grew, its complexity became a serious problem.

Researchers had to:
• Work with fragmented and hard-to-understand configurations
• Rely on personal experience to avoid mistakes
• Find errors late, often after studies were already live

This led to long onboarding, high mental load, and costly mistakes.
stellaris-ftue.solution:
The core workflows were redesigned as clear, step-by-step SaaS flows.

Complex logic and settings were made visible and easier to understand. Key decisions are made upfront, dependencies are clear, and built-in validation helps prevent errors — making the product easier to learn, safer to use, and ready to scale as a SaaS platform.

focusAreas.title: Logic visualization system
focusAreas.description: Developed a layered approach: simple conditions edit inline, complex logic reveals in a dedicated builder, and the full survey flow renders as a navigable diagram. Power users access everything; casual users see what they need.

focusAreas.title: QBank architecture
focusAreas.description: Redesigned the question library to support inheritance and variants. Master questions propagate changes to all instances while allowing local overrides — reducing duplication without limiting flexibility.

userImpact: Logic errors caught before deployment increased 3x
businessImpact: Design system reduced development time for new features
stellaris-ftue.takeaway: Progressive disclosure isn't about hiding complexity — it's about revealing it at the right moment. Expert tools should feel simple until users need the power.

stellaris-cloaking.title: FinOptima — AI-driven fraud detection platform for financial institutions
stellaris-cloaking.subtitle: USA · Fintech · Cybersecurity · B2B SaaS · Risk Intelligence
stellaris-cloaking.context:
Financial institutions face growing synthetic identity fraud while relying on fragmented verification tools and opaque risk signals.

Fraud detection operated as a separate security layer rather than an embedded operational decision system.
stellaris-cloaking.myRole: Senior Product Designer responsible for MVP workflow architecture, risk-decision UX, AI explainability patterns, and cross-team alignment between product, AI, and compliance.
stellaris-cloaking.problem:
Risk signals arrived from disconnected sources, investigations were manual, and decisions depended heavily on analyst intuition.

Limited traceability slowed approvals, increased exposure, and created inconsistent outcomes.
stellaris-cloaking.solution:
The MVP introduced a unified, explainable risk-decision workflow that aggregates AI signals, guides analyst investigations, and creates auditable outcomes in real time.

This established the operational foundation for today's production fraud-detection platform.

mvpWorkflow.intro: The MVP was structured around three operational screens:

screens.title: Monitoring dashboard
screens.description: Real-time overview of applications, statuses, and risk progression, designed for rapid triage and prioritization.

screens.title: Risk profile & investigation view
screens.description: Centralized identity data, anomaly signals, and recommended actions combined into a single explainable analyst decision surface.

screens.title: Verification evidence layer
screens.description: Document authenticity, biometric checks, and database validation supporting confident approval or escalation.

mvpWorkflow.outro: Together, these formed the minimal viable decision system required for safe real-world deployment.

userImpact: Clear, explainable risk at decision points
businessImpact: The MVP became the foundation of the current production platform.
stellaris-cloaking.reflection:
This project reinforced that AI products are not about models — they are about decisions. The challenge was defining the minimal operational system capable of safe real-world use, not just demonstrating technology.

In risk-critical systems, UX determines whether intelligence becomes real-world protection.
stellaris-cloaking.whyMatters: AI products are not about models — they are about decisions. The challenge was defining the minimal operational system capable of safe real-world use, not just demonstrating technology.

decathlon-travel.title: Design-to-Factory Collaborative Platform
decathlon-travel.subtitle: France · Fashion Tech · B2B / B2E SaaS
decathlon-travel.context: Fashion brands manage collections across designers, suppliers, and factories. Communication happens through email threads, PDFs, spreadsheets, and disconnected 3D or tech-pack files. Sample development, approvals, and cost updates are handled across multiple tools without a shared operational layer.
decathlon-travel.myRole: Senior Product Designer responsible for platform architecture, cross-functional workflow design, factory–designer communication systems, and operational visibility across collection development.
decathlon-travel.problem: Design feedback, material confirmations, and sample iterations were fragmented and difficult to track. Deadlines were managed manually, version history was unclear, and factories lacked structured visibility into priorities. Delays and misunderstandings increased operational risk and slowed production cycles.
decathlon-travel.solution: The platform introduced a unified design-to-factory workspace that centralizes 3D reviews, material validation, sample tracking, and deadline monitoring. Structured activity logs, status visibility, and traceable approvals transformed fragmented communication into a transparent, deadline-driven production system.

transformations.solution: Centralized 3D review with contextual comments and version traceability
Real-time delivery status: On Time / At Risk / Delayed

transformations.problem: Factories waiting for answers without visibility
transformations.solution: Action-based dashboard with Pending Approvals and Required Responses
Clear stage labeling: Prototype → Sample 01 → Sample 02 → Pre-Production
Activity log combining design decisions, confirmations, and production signals

userImpact: Clear visibility into what requires action
Structured feedback instead of scattered emails
Faster decision loops between designers and factories
decathlon-travel.reflection:
This project reinforced that collaboration design is not about messaging — it's about operational clarity.

The real challenge wasn't building a communication interface. It was designing a system where every comment, approval, and deadline becomes part of a structured production flow.

The platform transforms creative iteration and factory execution into one shared operational language.
decathlon-travel.whyMatters: This project demonstrates designing cross-organizational operational systems where UX decisions directly affect production timing, cost control, and accountability — not just usability metrics.

sampleWorkflow.intro: The platform supports the full sample development cycle — from initial design iteration to production confirmation. Depending on the stage (Prototype, Sample 01, Sample 02, Pre-Production), the level of validation changes: design feedback, material confirmation, feasibility checks, cost updates, and deadline validation.
sampleWorkflow.research:
To design this properly, it was necessary to deeply understand how sample development unfolds in reality — across emails, shared folders, supplier confirmations, and last-minute changes. This required mapping: who initiates decisions, who validates them, where delays typically occur, how factories signal risk, and how designers track iteration status.

Before digitalization, much of this logic existed in inboxes and informal conversations. Deadlines were tracked manually. Version history was unclear. Factories often waited for answers without visibility.
sampleWorkflow.outcome:
These observations directly shaped the platform's structure: 3D annotation tied to specific iterations, structured activity logs, clear sample stages, deadline-based risk indicators, and a centralized message center by collection.

The workflow was intentionally designed to reflect how teams already reason about development — by product, by sample stage, and by urgency — turning informal coordination into an operational system.

screens.title: 3D Review & Annotation
screens.description: Centralized 3D view with contextual comments tied to specific product areas. Each annotation tracks status (Under Review, Resolved), replies, and visual references — replacing scattered email feedback with structured, version-linked design reviews.

screens.title: Collection Message Center
screens.description: Filterable product list organized by collection and season. Each item shows dossier number, category, supplier, sample stage, due date, and real-time delivery status (On Time, At Risk, Delayed) — giving teams structured visibility across the full development pipeline.

screens.title: Factory Action Dashboard
screens.description: Operational overview surfacing collection progress, pending approvals, at-risk items, and overdue tasks. Designed for factories to see exactly what requires action — reducing wait times and improving response accountability.
